item.title: oh god my heart
item.description: The world will wake up to some devastating news: RJ Mitte ended his own life yesterday. From Bryan Cranston: I’m in deep despair as I write this tonight. RJ Mitte, my sweet son on Breaking Bad has died. I met him when he was only 14 years old when he was cast as Walter White Jr., a part he played with such joy and enthusiasm. Born with Cerebral Palsy, he never - ever - allowed that challenge to be an excuse for anything. He met the demanding shooting schedule head on with great determination. Always listening to the advice that his TV parents (Anna Gunn and myself) gave him - but being a teenager, sometimes mischievously ignoring the counsel in order to learn the hard way… He was one of the stars of a hit TV show - but still a kid. That kid was pretty raw when we started shooting the pilot in February of 2007, but little by little we watched him grow into a really fine actor. He parlayed his experience on the show to be a vocal advocate for performers with disabilities, and was the head of a philanthropic organization with a focus on helping the disabled community. All that promise and potential now is such a loss. It is especially devastating to hear that he took his own life. Why? We were texting each other just a few weeks ago - figuring out when we could meet for lunch. I don’t know if that lunch would have changed his future… But I do know that I loved him, and thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series, and after the spotlight on Breaking Bad dimmed… I’ll miss you, son. I can’t stop there without imploring anyone who is contemplating suicide to please call for the support you need at 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (https://988lifeline.org/). There is hope.

item.title: An engineer built a Flock-like camera to detect police cars, says officers visited him afterward - They worried his $180 prototype could reveal officers' homes, work schedules and daily routines
item.description: A Canadian software engineer who built a camera to identify police cars says two officers came to his home to ask why he was tracking them. They were concerned that repeated observations could expose their routines – the same information that makes searchable vehicle records useful to police and troubling to people being watched. Anthony Sistilli described Peel Regional Police's visit last month in a YouTube video that he recently posted. His project uses automatic license plate recognition, or ALPR – the technology police use to record passing vehicles and search for them later. But Sistilli designed his camera to pick out police vehicles rather than collect plates from all traffic. Sistilli built the prototype with a $180 camera and used AI coding tools to develop its software. The first version struggled to process 4K footage while identifying vehicles and reading their license plates. He lowered the resolution and split the work into two stages: first detect a police car, then try to read its plate. That change reduced the amount of footage the plate-recognition software had to examine. It also made vehicle classification a prerequisite for capturing license plate data. The system would attempt a read only after deciding that a vehicle was a police car. Sistilli said the officers were polite but worried that someone could use the information to target them. He told them those were the same concerns civilians had about license-plate surveillance. According to his account, the officers said stronger disclosure requirements could reveal details of active investigations. The results were modest. An hour-long test produced two images of police vehicles, but their plates were difficult to read. The demonstration showed a working concept, not a dependable tracking system. However, it did attract the attention of local police after Sistilli posted videos of the project. https://www.techspot.com/news/114167-engineer-built-flock-like-camera-detect-police-cars.html https://www.youtube.com/embed/ncCf00M7Axk
